fields.title: République démocratique du Congo - Initiative conjointe de suivi des marchés (ICSM) - octobre 2026
fields.body:
**MESSAGES CLÉS**

• Le coût médian du MEB, calculé sur l’ensemble des marchés évalués, a augmenté de 10% entre septembre et octobre. Il s’élevait à 464'921 francs congolais (FC) et variait de 285'841 FC au marché Kapulo de Nyunzu (Tanganyika) à 1'360'560 FC au marché Nyasi dans le territoire de Walikale (NordKivu).

• Cette hausse est principalement portée par le panier alimentaire (+15%). Le prix médian de la farine de maïs a augmenté de 17% (2'128 FC/kg), celui de la farine de manioc de 21% (1'727 FC/kg) et celui des haricots de 12% (3'448 FC/kg). Le coût du panier EHA/combustible est resté stable et celui des AME a légèrement augmenté (+3%).

• À Masisi, le coût médian du MEB a augmenté de 24% entre septembre et octobre, principalement sous l’effet de la hausse du panier alimentaire (+40%). Une augmentation a été observée dans 6 des 7 marchés suivis, notamment au Marché central (+23%), à Lushebere (+21%) et à Nyabiondo (+20%). Les hausses les plus importantes concernaient la farine de manioc (+50%), les haricots (+40%) et la farine de maïs (+38%). Cette hausse intervient dans un contexte d'insécurité persistante ayant affecté l'activité commerciale et l'accès aux marchés.

• La fonctionnalité des marchés s'est améliorée à Goma en octobre. Les marchés Alanine et Birere sont passés d'une mauvaise fonctionnalité à une fonctionnalité limitée, surtout grâce à une meilleure accessibilité. À Alanine, 29 des 33 commerçants interrogés n'ont signalé aucun problème de sécurité. À Birere, aucun commerçant n'en a signalé (0/29).

• À l'inverse, La fonctionnalité des marchés s’est dégradée dans plusieurs provinces. 5 marchés sont passés d’une fonctionnalité limitée à une mauvaise fonctionnalité et 6 d’une mauvaise fonctionnalité à des problèmes graves. À Kapulo, tous les commerçants interrogés (6/6) ont signalé l’indisponibilité de certains produits, tandis qu’à Maendeleo, 28 commerçants sur 69 ont déclaré que le marché n’était pas pleinement fonctionnel.

fields.title: Gavi signs agreement with Serum Institute of India to secure rapid access to Bundibugyo vaccines
fields.body:
- ## Advance purchase commitment from Gavi secures access to up to 1.5 million doses of ChAdOx1 BDBV, a Bundibugyo candidate vaccine developed jointly by Serum Institute of India and the Oxford Vaccine Group at the University of Oxford
- ## The agreement is funded through Gavi’s First Response Fund, with supply remaining conditional on clinical trial results, as well as the candidate vaccine securing necessary regulatory approvals and policy recommendations
- ## Dr Sania Nishtar, CEO of Gavi: *“For the second public health emergency of international concern since its launch, the First Response Fund is functioning as designed – securing early and rapid access to vaccines so that communities can be protected as quickly as possible.”*

**Geneva, 24 November 2026** – Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance today announced that it had signed an advance purchase commitment with the Serum Institute of India (SII) and Serum Life Sciences to secure access to up to 1.5 million doses of ChAdOx1 BDBV – a candidate vaccine against the Bundibugyo species of Ebolavirus. These doses, funded through Gavi’s [First Response Fund](https://www.gavi.org/news/media-room/gavi-commits-us-50-million-bundibugyo-ebolavirus-vaccines-and-outbreak-response)\* (FRF), would be procured in the event of successful clinical trial results, regulatory approvals, and appropriate policy recommendations for the vaccine’s use.

“For the second public health emergency of international concern since its launch, the First Response Fund is functioning as designed – securing early and rapid access to vaccines so that communities can be protected as quickly as possible,” said **Dr Sania Nishtar, CEO of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.** “As the Ebola outbreak continues to devastate communities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, we must act with urgency to ensure the regulatory pathways are in place to quickly roll out this vaccine candidate if the clinical trials show positive results. This is critical to saving lives and keeping the world safe.”

To date, the current Ebola outbreak has resulted in more than 11,600 cases and more than 5,700 deaths – the vast majority in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. ChAdOx1 BDBV is one of two novel Bundibugyo vaccine candidates that WHO has recommended for clinical testing in the on-going outbreak.

In the event that the candidate vaccine secures the necessary regulatory approvals and WHO SAGE policy recommendations following its trials, Gavi’s advance purchase commitment means that doses can be made available to affected populations quickly. SII has already manufactured the drug substance for more than half a million doses of the candidate vaccine to enable rapid access.

Today’s announcement is part of [Gavi’s overall support for the response to the on-going Ebola outbreak.](https://www.gavi.org/news/media-room/gavi-commits-additional-funding-ebola-response) Up to US$ 40 million from the First Response Fund (FRF) mechanism has been dedicated to support vaccine access deals such as this advance purchase commitment. An additional US$ 10 million from the FRF – of which US$ 6 million has already been committed or disbursed to the DRC, Uganda, Africa CDC, WHO and UNICEF – is helping to protect routine immunisation services in impacted communities and frontline health workers. Ervebo, an existing Ebola vaccine which is licensed for use against the Ebola Zaire strain of the disease, is also being deployed under clinical research protocols. Gavi has made an additional investment of US$7 million to provide 70,000 doses of the existing Ervebo from the Gavi-funded global stockpile. These doses are currently being administered to affected populations in the DRC under WHO compassionate emergency use protocols.

**Notes to Editors**

*\*The **First Response Fund (FRF)** is made possible by the governments that have invested in this crucial part of Gavi’s outbreak and pandemic response capacity. Gavi recognises the critical support of the **United States, Japan, Italy, Germany, Norway and France**, whose commitments helped to ensure Gavi’s $500m FRF was fully funded.*

The FRF was also leveraged to rapidly respond to the 2024 Mpox emergency. Read more [here](https://reliefweb.int/news/media-room/gavi-delivers-largest-shipment-yet-drc-support-international-mpox-response).

**About Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance**

Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance is a public-private partnership that helps vaccinate more than half the world’s children against some of the world’s deadliest diseases. The Vaccine Alliance brings together developing country and donor governments, the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the World Bank, the vaccine industry, technical agencies, civil society, the Gates Foundation and other private sector partners. View the full list of donor governments and other leading organisations that fund [Gavi’s work here](https://reliefweb.int/investing-gavi/funding/donor-profiles).

Since its inception in 2000, Gavi has helped to immunise a whole generation – over 1.3 billion children – and prevented more than 23 million future deaths, helping to halve child mortality in 78 lower income countries. Gavi also plays a key role in improving global health security by supporting health systems as well as funding global stockpiles for Ebola, cholera, meningococcal, mpox and yellow fever vaccines. After more than two decades of progress, Gavi is now focused on protecting the next generation, above all the zero-dose children who have not received even a single vaccine shot. The Vaccine Alliance employs innovative finance and the latest technology – from drones to biometrics – to save lives, prevent outbreaks before they can spread and help countries on the road to self-sufficiency. Learn more at [www.gavi.org](https://reliefweb.int/homepage) and connect with us on [Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/gavi.org), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/GAVI/), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/gavialliance/), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/Gavi/), [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@gavialliance), [X](https://twitter.com/gavi) and [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@Gavi).

fields.title: Direct Relief Delivers 53 Tons of Medical Aid to Combat Record DRC Ebola Outbreak
fields.body:
*With more than 11,000 confirmed cases reported by the World Health Organization, insecurity in Ituri and North Kivu continues to challenge containment efforts. Direct Relief has provided PPE, diagnostic tools, and chronic care medications across Congo, Uganda, and South Sudan to local health organizations on the front lines.*

By [**Noah Smith**](https://www.directrelief.org/author/nsmith/)

An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has killed 5,630 people and seen 11,504 confirmed cases, according to the World Health Organization’s Nov. 16 update.

Children account for more than a quarter of confirmed cases and one-third of deaths. Seven in 10 children under 5 with confirmed Ebola have died, according to WHO.

The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which no vaccines are currently licensed. Declared in May, this is the deadliest outbreak in the country’s history.

WHO said Tuesday that 400 to 500 new cases continue to be reported weekly, despite progress in slowing transmission in several early outbreak epicenters.

Ituri province remains the outbreak’s epicenter, although transmission has also spread through neighboring North Kivu and other provinces.

Insecurity has increasingly disrupted containment efforts. An attack on Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu earlier this month killed 66 civilians, including three health workers, according to WHO. Health facilities were looted and burned, and more than 1,000 contacts of Ebola patients were lost to follow-up.

WHO said on Nov. 17 that about two in every three confirmed Ebola deaths occur outside treatment centers. The agency said that points to delays in identifying infections.

Direct Relief has delivered **53 tons of Ebola-specific medical aid valued at approximately $15 million** to partners in Congo, Uganda and South Sudan as of Nov. 5, including more than 425,000 items of personal protective equipment.

Since May 1, Direct Relief has shipped about $47.3 million in medical aid overall to countries affected by the [Ebola outbreak](https://www.directrelief.org/emergency/drc-ebola-outbreak-2026/?_gl=1%2A1kkgw37%2A_up%2AMQ..%2A_ga%2AMTU4NDY0NDE2OC4xNzk1MDQzODM2%2A_ga_WYKLEGJW76%2AczE3OTUwNDM4MzYkbzEkZzAkdDE3OTUwNDM4MzYkajYwJGwwJGgxODcxNjE3NTcz). The outbreak has also [disrupted routine care](https://www.directrelief.org/2026/07/the-patients-ebola-statistics-dont-count/) for people with other illnesses.

The assistance from Direct Relief includes:

- Essential medicines, intravenous fluids, antibiotics, diagnostic supplies and medications for chronic conditions, helping health facilities maintain routine services while responding to Ebola.
- A 10-ton shipment containing more than $490,000 in **essential medicines, medical supplies and protective equipment arrived in Kinshasa on Nov. 2 for VillageReach**, with supplies designated for health facilities in Ituri, Tshopo and Haut-Uele provinces.
- Direct Relief has also supported **Première Urgence Internationale with medical supplies and protective equipment** for health facilities in Ituri.
- The organization provided a $50,000 emergency grant to **Humanitarian Action for Africa** to strengthen Ebola preparedness in North and South Kivu, including disease surveillance, case management, medical supply management, and community outreach.
- Last week, Direct Relief shipped approximately 3,800 pounds of **protective equipment to the International Organization for Migration in Congo**. The shipment included approximately 4,500 protective coveralls and more than 15,000 N95 respirators to support health screenings and disease surveillance along transit routes, at border crossings and in displacement sites.

Other partners include **Jericho Road, Mulago National Referral Hospital in Uganda, and Association des Diabétiques (Diabetic Association)**.

**Vaccine Research and Regional Risks**

The WHO said that it expects two vaccine candidates designed for the Bundibugyo virus to join an ongoing trial in Congo in the coming weeks. The trial began in October with Ervebo, a vaccine licensed against a different virus that causes Ebola. Separately, more than 900 people have enrolled in studies of potential treatments.

Outside Congo, Kenya has reported nine cases and two deaths, while Nigeria recorded one imported case. Kenya’s last patient has been discharged, and Nigeria’s patient has recovered.

Despite expanded laboratory capacity and nearly 2,000 treatment beds, continued transmission and limited access to affected communities remain significant challenges.

Health organizations are working to strengthen infection prevention and clinical care while maintaining essential medical services in communities affected by the outbreak.

fields.title: "Families are under enormous pressure because of Ebola, and women and girls are bearing much of the cost" – UNICEF
fields.body:
This is a summary of what was said by Dr. Douglas Noble, UNICEF Global Lead for Public Health Emergencies and Global Incident Manager for Ebola – to whom quoted text may be attributed – at today's press briefing at the Palais des Nations in Geneva



**GENEVA, 24 November 2026** – “I've just wrapped up a trip to Beni, Butembo, and Bunia, in eastern DRC.

“The response has made considerable progress since my last visit in May, but much remains to be done, and the outbreak’s wider impact on families and communities is becoming clearer.

“In Bunia, I visited a safe space for women and girls next to an Ebola treatment centre and joined a focus group at a nearby church. Both are part of efforts to address violence against women and girls during the outbreak, and both are places where people can gather and speak safely. I learned how violence was increasing and how fear of Ebola was leading to women’s movements being restricted, potentially exposing them to violence and abuse.

“It reinforced for me that the consequences of an outbreak extend far beyond infection and death, and that our response must recognize and address these wider impacts.

“Today, we're releasing preliminary findings from what is, to our knowledge, the first real-time surveillance of violence against women and adolescent girls during an active disease outbreak. UNICEF is carrying out this work with SOFEPADI, a Congolese women-led organization, and Washington University in St. Louis.

“So far, we've spoken to 1,062 women and adolescent girls across five health zones in Ituri. We're also hearing from young people through U-Report, UNICEF's digital platform, and talking to frontline workers.

"This surveillance is helping us understand where risks are increasing while there's still time to do something about it. And what we're already hearing is concerning.

“Nearly 6 in 10 women and adolescent girls surveyed said violence and abuse had started or increased in their lives since the Ebola outbreak began.

“More than a third described someone taking more control over their lives, followed by emotional and psychological abuse. Others reported physical and sexual violence.

“Seven in 10 live in households that have been through isolation, quarantine, or contact tracing. Of them, nearly 2 in 3 reported new or increased violence. Nine in 10 linked it to the stress and fear this outbreak has brought into their homes.

“I want to be very clear about something. Isolation, quarantine, and contact tracing are absolutely critical to stopping Ebola. But what these findings are telling us is that families are under enormous pressure because of Ebola, and women and girls are bearing much of the cost.

"I raised this issue during my mission in-country, and there was real interest in addressing it. UNICEF and our partners will follow up to ensure that the needs and protection of women and girls remain central to the response.

"Since June, UNICEF and partners have supported more than 3,300 survivors of gender-based violence in Ituri and North Kivu. But protecting women and children is one of the most underfunded parts of this response. Right now, the funding gap is 76 per cent.

"We must, therefore, keep services for women and girls open, accessible and funded, and open new ones where Ebola is spreading. Ensuring the safety of women and girls should be an integral part of this response. And, this kind of surveillance should be built into every outbreak response from day one.

“Now, none of this would exist without SOFEPADI, whose teams are from and in these communities every day. I’ll hand over now to Sandrine Lusamba, SOFEPADI’s National Coordinator.”

\#####

fields.title: Nearly 6 in 10 women and adolescent girls surveyed in Ebola-hit Ituri report increase in violence and abuse [EN/AR]
fields.body:
**Findings show a worsening parallel crisis for women and girls, including emotional and psychological abuse, controlling behaviour, and physical and sexual violence**

**KINSHASA/BUNIA/NEW YORK, 24 November 2026** – Nearly 6 in 10 women and adolescent girls aged 15 and above surveyed in Ituri in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported an increase or emergence of violence and abuse in their lives since the Ebola outbreak began.

Drawn from the first ever real-time surveillance of violence against women and girls during an infectious disease outbreak – led by UNICEF with the women-led organization SOFEPADI and Washington University in St. Louis – the findings point to how the outbreak is affecting women's and adolescent girls' safety at home and in their communities.

“Women and girls are facing a growing threat of violence and abuse on top of a deadly disease outbreak and continued conflict in eastern DRC,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell. “Too often, in the most impacted areas, there are no protective spaces outside the home that they can safely access.”

Based on 1,062 interviews with women and adolescent girls between 28 August and 15 October, the findings point to an increase or emergence of at least one form of violence and abuse. More than a third of those surveyed reported growing control over where they could go, their money, and their phones, as well as emotional and psychological abuse. Physical and sexual violence were also reported.

According to the findings, 7 in 10 respondents state they live in households that have experienced at least one public health response measure, such as isolation, quarantine, or contact tracing. Of those that also reported an increase in violence and abuse, 9 in 10 named stress and fear brought on by the outbreak as contributing factors.

Almost half of the women and adolescent girls who tried to access care and support services could not. Frontline workers reported that some women and girls are limiting their own movements to avoid infection, while others are being kept close to home by family members or others. Some of the centres and services they once relied on have closed or been repurposed. Respondents also cited shame, fear of the perpetrator, and lack of trust.

Where safe spaces for women and girls affected by, or at risk of, violence remain open and accessible, demand for them is growing. For example, visits to eight safe spaces run by SOFEPADI in Ituri rose by 200 per cent, from 1,183 visits between January to March to 3,548 visits between July to September.

In a separate UNICEF poll of around 11,500 young people in Ituri through U-Report – UNICEF’s digital platform for youth to share their views on issues affecting them – nearly half of all respondents said they see greater risks of violence for women and girls since the outbreak began. Physical and sexual violence were the most commonly cited concerns.

Women and girls carry more of the outbreak’s risk. Caring for sick relatives, preparing loved ones for burial, and frequent trips to health facilities, including with ill children, raises their risk of infection. All of this comes on top of an already fragile situation, where years of conflict and displacement had left women and girls facing alarming levels of gender-based violence long before the outbreak began. Now, many report even more violence at home and in their communities.

Since the outbreak began, UNICEF and partners have assisted more than 3,300 survivors of gender-based violence in Ituri and North Kivu and provided mental health and psychosocial support to close to 175,000 people between June and October. But protecting children and women, including gender-based violence services, remains among the most underfunded parts of the response, with a funding gap of 76 per cent.

The results of the surveillance are being shared with Ebola response coordinators to inform decisions as UNICEF continues to call on government authorities, response partners, and donors to:

- Make the safety of women and girls a measure of an effective Ebola response. Work with local women’s organizations to spot rising risks early, act, and avoid putting women and girls at risk or preventing them from getting help.
- Keep services for women and girls open, accessible, and funded at scale throughout the outbreak, and establish new services in Ebola hotspots. As risks rise and demand for support grows, gender-based violence services, including safe spaces, must be able to meet it.
- Scale surveillance of violence into this current Ebola response and build it in future public health emergency preparedness and response. With women’s organizations formally part of surveillance, and safeguards for confidentiality and safety built in, monitoring must start as soon as an outbreak begins.

"There is no excuse for violence and abuse against women and girls,” said Russell. “Protection must be part of the Ebola response, and it must be informed by what women and girls tell us. That includes prioritizing prevention and services for survivors.”

**Partner quotes**

"Since the outbreak began, more and more women and girls are coming to our safe spaces, looking to be heard, protected, and supported, without fear or stigma. Safe spaces must stay open and be properly resourced throughout the response. Surveillance and support should be extended to other areas at risk," said Sandrine Lusamba, National Coordinator of SOFEPADI.

"When women explain why violence has started or worsened, many point to the fear and pressure this outbreak has brought into their homes. Those pressures can be anticipated. Keeping services open, establishing new services, and listening to women as the response unfolds can stop that pressure from turning into harm," said Dr. Lindsay Stark, Co-Director of the Center on Violence and Health at the Bursky School of Public Health, Washington University in St. Louis.

\#####

*Notes to editors:*

Read more about the Ebola outbreak VAWG surveillance [here](https://www.unicef.org/media/186251/file).

fields.title: Fiche d’information : Tendances observées de juillet à septembre 2026 issues des analyses du Groupe de travail d’analyse de crises et qualité de réponse (GTACQ) - Provinces du Sud-Kivu, Nord-Kivu et Ituri (juillet - septembre 2026)
fields.body:
**Messages clés**

• Besoins humanitaires: Bien qu’une amélioration relative des besoins ait été observée dans certaines ZS au troisième trimestre 2026, les besoins demeuraient particulièrement critiques à Mweso, Mulungu et Fataki. Les déplacements massifs de population à Masisi, Kibirizi, Birambizo, Fizi, Kalehe, Itombwe, Minembwe, Minova et Boga, combinés à la hausse du coût du MEB dans plusieurs ZS, continuaient d’exacerber les vulnérabilités humanitaires.

• Accès humanitaire :les contraintes d’accès demeuraient particulièrement sévères à Pinga, Nyiragongo, Kibirizi, Fizi, Fataki et Bambu, toutes classées en hotspots lifesaving avec un score d’accès maximal tandis que le Nord-Kivu restait la province la plus affectée.

• Gaps de la réponse : les gaps critiques de la réponse persistaient dans plusieurs zones de santé de l’est de la RDC, notamment à Mweso, Nyiragongo, Pinga, Kayna, Kalole, Kaniola, Tchomia et Bambu, où les besoins identifiés demeuraient entièrement non couverts malgré certaines améliorations du contexte opérationnel.

**Faits saillants**

- Les affrontements armés dans les territoires de Kalehe, Walungu, Uvira, Fizi et Shabunda ont provoqué le déplacement de plus de 100 000 personnes, accentuant les besoins en protection, abris, alimentation et services essentiels.
- Le choléra demeure une préoccupation majeure avec plus de 16 700 cas et 242 décès enregistrés depuis le début de l’année malgré les efforts de réponse.

fields.title: MSF DRC: Child dies while awaiting medical evacuation as intensified clashes disrupt access to care in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory
fields.body:
**23 November, 2026** – Intensifying armed clashes in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory, North Kivu, have put civilians at serious risk since 18 November. Those clashes have led to the tragic death of a 15-year-old child who suffered from bullet wounds while awaiting urgent referral, blocked due to the ongoing hostilities. Médecins Sans Frontières / Doctors without Borders (MSF), which supports several health facilities in the area, is deeply concerned about the disruption of essential healthcare and the safety of affected communities. The organisation calls on all parties to the conflict to take immediate measures to protect civilians, healthcare facilities, patients and humanitarian personnel.

On 18 November, clashes between the Front pour la Refondation de la Nation (FRN) and Wazalendo armed groups intensified in Nyabiondo, Masisi territory, North Kivu. Many people sought refuge at the MSF-supported Nyabiondo Referral Health Centre, despite stray bullets occasionally reaching the facility's perimeter. The deteriorating security situation also forced MSF teams working in surrounding areas to take shelter and temporarily suspend their activities. ​

As of 21 November, the Nyabiondo Referral Health Centre has treated 19 people with conflict-related injuries, including several children, while the violent clashes continue. Three patients requiring urgent medical evacuation to the MSF-supported Masisi General Referral Hospital for specialised care remained stranded for nearly 24 hours because of the ongoing hostilities, placing their lives at serious risk. Tragically, a 15-year-old child who had sustained multiple gunshot wounds died while waiting urgent referral for surgery.

“This death illustrates the devastating impact of insecurity and obstacles to care on people trapped in conflict," says Olivier Pennec, MSF project coordinator in Masisi. "No child should die from gunshot wounds because they were unable to access the care they need."

The latest escalation takes place against a backdrop of prolonged insecurity, food scarcity and repeated displacement. Several front lines are surrounding Nyabiondo. Recurring clashes along roads in the area have forced successive waves of people to flee their homes and seek refuge in increasingly precarious conditions, with limited access to healthcare.

"We demand that all parties involved in the conflict act right now to keep civilians safe, along with healthcare structures, patients and aid workers," says Pennec. "Protecting people and keeping healthcare accessible has to come first, even while the fighting goes on."

**END**

*In Masisi, MSF provides comprehensive support to Masisi General Referral Hospital and five health facilities, ensuring access to primary and secondary healthcare, including emergency medical and surgical care, medical and psychological support to survivors of sexual violence, responses to disease outbreaks such as measles and cholera, and the support of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) activities.*

## **Zoe Bennell**

Press Officer (Features), MSF UK

fields.title: Situation d'urgence au Tchad I Mise à jour des arrivées du Soudan (22 nov. 2026)
fields.body: Depuis le début du conflit au Soudan en avril 2023, la CNARR, le HCR et l'OIM identifient et enregistrent les réfugiés soudanais et les migrants tchadiens retournés en provenance du Darfour. Une estimation de 1 070 847\* personnes nécessitant une assistance humanitaire a été établie. Pour garantir leur protection, une opération de dénombrement a été lancée le long de la frontière, permettant la collecte des données essentielles sur les réfugiés pour une assistance ciblée. En parallèle, la relocalisation depuis les sites spontanés vers des sites aménagés est mise en œuvre et permet de poursuivre l’enregistrement biométrique individuel des réfugiés.

fields.title: Evaluation conjointe des besoins en matière d’Education et Protection RDC-2026
fields.body:
Le rapport de l’évaluation conjointe des besoins d’Education et de Protection menée en collaboration avec le secteur de la Protection met en évidence les résultats suivants :

- Taux d’abandon de 12,5 % au cours de l’année scolaire 2025-2026, principalement lié aux difficultés socio-économiques des ménages, aux déplacements forcés, aux travaux domestiques, ainsi qu’aux mariages et grossesses précoces.
- 131 établissements sur 266 (50 %) rapportent des absences scolaires liées à la gestion des menstruations.
- 76 responsables d’établissements sur 266 (28%) affirment que les établissements ont subi des pillages ou vols perpétrés par des groupes armés depuis le début de l’année 2026, tandis que 47 sur 266 (18%) ont relevé l’occupation de salles de classe par des forces ou groupes armés.
- L’inclusion des enfants en situation de handicap demeure limitée, avec peu de mesures spécifiques favorisant leur participation et leur maintien à l’école.
- Seuls 51 établissements sur 266 (19 %) disposent d’un accès à l’eau potable provenant de leur principale source d’approvisionnement.
- 114 établissements (43 %) ne disposent pas de latrines séparées pour les filles et les garçons.
- 101 établissements sur 266 (38 %) signalent la présence d’enfants présentant des signes de détresse psychosociale, notamment des cauchemars, une tristesse persistante, une anxiété élevée, de la fatigue extrême, des comportements violents ou de l’isolement.
- Seuls 70 établissements sur 266 (26%) disposent d’un mécanisme de référencement VBG adapté aux enfants et permettant l’orientation vers des services spécialisés.

Malgré ces défis, les consultations avec les enfants montrent que l’école reste perçue comme un espace de protection, de stabilité et d’espoir. Comme l’a souligné un enfant de 8 à 11 ans : « **A l’école, on étudie et on oublie la guerre**. »

fields.title: Disease Outbreak News: Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus- Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya and Nigeria (20 November 2026)
fields.body:
**Situation at a glance**

Since the publication of the previous Disease Outbreak News on 6 November 2026, additional confirmed cases and deaths have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. While some areas have seen a slight decline in cases, sustained, high-level transmission continues overall in the country. As of 17 November 2026, a total of 11 613 confirmed cases, including 5678 deaths (crude case fatality ratio: 48.9%), have been reported across 68 health zones in eight provinces, with active transmission ongoing in 48 health zones. Ituri and Nord Kivu remain the most affected provinces, while Sud-Kivu and Sud Ubangi have not reported cases for more than 42 days. The high proportion of deaths occurring in communities, meaning outside of dedicated treatment centres, especially among young children, continues to highlight challenges in early case detection and timely access to appropriate care. Of the 720 deaths reported since 28 October (last three weeks), 452 occurred in communities and 268 in treatment centres. Since the last Disease Outbreak News, no new cases have been reported from Kenya or Nigeria; and no new country has reported confirmed cases. Both countries have started a 42-day countdown to declare the end of their outbreaks. However, the high-level transmission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo calls for continued need for readiness in the region, including cross-border surveillance, points of entry monitoring, timely case detection and coordinated preparedness and response measures. Six months into the outbreak of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the response has expanded significantly, but further scale up is needed, with rising insecurity remaining the greatest obstacle to the expansion of operations. The next phase must prioritize quality, reach and community trust, alongside sustained funding, coordination and security to save lives and end the outbreak. On 18 November 2026, the Director-General of WHO, concurring with the advice of the IHR Emergency Committee formulated at its third meeting, on 17 November 2026, determined that the event continues to constitute a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC). Updated recommendations to the government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and all other States Parties will be issued in the coming days.

**Description of the situation**

Cases have been reported in five countries since the declaration of the outbreak on 15 May 2026: the Democratic Republic of the Congo, France, Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda. The outbreaks in France and Uganda have been controlled since August, while Kenya and Nigeria continue with heightened surveillance as they count down to 42 days, completing two maximum incubation periods since the last confirmed cases were either discharged or medically evacuated from the country.

On 26 October 2026, Switzerland reported the medical evacuation of the case, who received medical care in Geneva, Switzerland. The patient recovered and was discharged on 11 November testing PCR-negative for Bundibugyo virus for a second time.

On 18 November 2026, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland reported that a medically evacuated health and care worker from the Democratic Republic of the Congo had recovered and been discharged from hospital.

**Democratic Republic of the Congo**

An additional 945 confirmed cases, including 480 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since the previous [Disease Outbreak News](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON625) was published.

In the last 21-day period, as of 17 November, 1417 new confirmed cases were reported, with Ituri accounting for 668 (13% decrease) cases, Nord Kivu for 635 (8% increase) cases, Haut-Uélé for 90 (13% increase) cases, Tshopo for 20 (47% decrease) cases and Nord-Ubangi for four cases. No new cases were reported in Bas-Uélé, Sud Kivu or Sud-Ubangi during that period.

As of 17 November, cumulative confirmed cases have reached 11 613, including 5678 deaths and 3148 recoveries. The overall crude CFR is 48.9%.

Confirmed cases have now been identified in 68 health zones across eight provinces. Forty-eight of the 68 affected health zones reported at least one new case during the preceding 21 days, while 20 reported no recent cases. Beni, Bunia, and Mandima have reported the highest number of cases and deaths in the preceding 21 days. Ituri remains the most extensively affected province, with 28 of 36 health zones reporting cases during this outbreak, followed by Nord Kivu (17/34), Haut-Uélé (8/13), Tshopo (7/23), Bas-Uélé (4/11), Nord-Ubangi (2/11), Sud Kivu (1/34) and Sud-Ubangi (1/16). Watsa in Haut-Uélé province is the most recently affected health zone, reporting 11 confirmed cases.

Six months into the BVD outbreak, the response has expanded significantly, but transmission remains persistent and geographically widespread. WHO, the national Government and partners have strengthened surveillance, treatment, laboratory capacity and community engagement, yet high community mortality, insecurity, displacement and a fragile health system continue to undermine progress.

The next phase will need to focus on scaling up, but also on improving the reach, quality and impact of the response. Early detection, quality care, contact tracing, infection prevention and community trust remain critical. Sustained funding, strong coordination and safe access to communities will be essential.

The third International Health Regulations (IHR) Emergency Committee meeting regarding the epidemic of BVD in the Democratic Republic of the Congo took place on 17 November. Following the advice of the Committee, the Director-General agreed that the ongoing outbreak remains a PHEIC. Updated recommendations to the government of the DRC and all other States Parties will be issued in the coming days and reported in the next Disease Outbreak News publication.

While Nord Kivu reported the highest number of cases in the last seven days (235 cases (40% increase compared to the previous seven days) as of 17 November), Ituri remains the most affected province since the outbreak was declared, with 7946 cumulative confirmed cases and 3751 deaths, with CFR of 47%. Nord Kivu follows with 2996 confirmed cases and 1654 deaths, and continues to record the highest provincial CFR, at 55%. Haut-Uélé has reported 534 cases and 231 deaths, while Tshopo has recorded 109 cases and 35 deaths. The less-affected provinces continue to report substantially fewer cases, but transmission persists in several of them. The continued occurrence of cases across multiple provinces shows that the outbreak remains geographically active even as intensity varies between health zones. Sud-Kivu and Sud Ubangi have not reported cases for more than 42 days.

As of 17 November 2026, the average proportion of contacts seen daily over the previous 14-day period is 81%, remaining below the required threshold of 95% for a daily average of the proportion of contacts seen over the previous 14-day period. Two provinces were at or above the 95% threshold: Bas-Uele (100%, 56/56) and Nord-Ubangi (99%, 140/138) Five provinces were below the threshold: Haut-Uélé (86%; 1741/1495), Ituri (86% (9564/11 104), Nord-Kivu (77%; 16 015/12 313), Tshopo (68%; 720/526), and Sud-Ubangi (63%; 127/80). Strengthened contact follow-up is required, particularly in provinces below the target, to achieve the minimum threshold of 95%.

**Kenya**

As of 17 November 2026, the cumulative confirmed cases reported in Kenya are nine, including two deaths, with a crude CFR of 22.2%. All eight secondary cases were epidemiologically linked to the imported index case and associated with one cluster (four family members of the index case and four health and care workers). All seven hospitalized cases have recovered and been discharged (the last case was discharged on 11 November). A 42-day countdown is underway and includes heightened surveillance.

There is currently no evidence of transmission outside this cluster, and there have been no new confirmed cases since 19 October 2026. Additionally, all eight secondary cases were already under quarantine as known contacts when they developed symptoms.

As of 17 November, of the 135 cumulative contacts identified since the first confirmed case, eight subsequently became confirmed cases and nine contacts left Kenya (relevant National IHR Focal Points were notified). All have completed the 21-day follow-up on 11 November 2026.

**Nigeria**

On 20 October 2026, Nigeria reported one laboratory-confirmed imported case of BVD in the Federal Capital Territory Abuja. On 26 October 2026, [Switzerland reported the medical evacuation of the case](https://www.admin.ch/en/newnsb/hKpTLMT8HgXi), who received medical care in Geneva, Switzerland. The patient recovered and was discharged on 11 November, following two PCR-negative test results for Bundibugyo virus.

As of 13 November, a cumulative of 62 contacts had been identified in Nigeria for follow-up and all the contacts have completed the 21-day follow-up period. National authorities, with support from WHO and partners, have intensified contact tracing, case investigation and infection prevention and control measures, including the provision of essential supplies and personal protective equipment for health workers. Investigations are ongoing to establish the likely source of infection and reconstruct the travel and exposure history of the imported case. WHO has urged countries across the region to strengthen surveillance, laboratory diagnostic capacity, rapid response readiness and cross-border preparedness to mitigate the risk of further transmission.

**Epidemiology**

Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the *Orthoebolavirus* species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir.

Human infection is thought to initially occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are inadequate, and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals.

The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations.

The CFR from the previous two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively.

Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification and investigation, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD.

Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission.

**Public health response**

For detailed information about the ongoing public health response actions by the Ministry of Health, WHO and partners please refer to the latest situation reports published by the WHO Regional Office for Africa: [Ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo | WHO | Regional Office for Africa](https://www.afro.who.int/health-topics/ebola-disease/outbreak-drc-26).

**Democratic Republic of the Congo**

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in collaboration with WHO and partners, are continuing to implement and coordinate extensive public health measures. These include disease surveillance; laboratory testing; IPC; clinical care; community engagement; research; logistics; and support for response interventions and essential health services, including for the ongoing concurrent humanitarian crisis; engaging donors and mobilizing additional resources to address critical funding gaps and sustain response operations across affected and at-risk areas. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak.

**Kenya**

On 11 November 2026, Kenya discharged its last confirmed BVD case after two negative tests, released the remaining contacts from quarantine, and began the 42-day countdown to declaring the end of the outbreak. Following the start of the 42-day countdown, Kenya has maintained cross-border surveillance and screening at all designated points of entry.

**Nigeria**

Nigeria has maintained a high level of alert for BVD since the outbreak began in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in May 2026. As of 13 November, all identified contacts had completed the 21-day follow-up period.

Following the medical evacuation of the case on 26 October, the country is continuing with the 42-days countdown to declare the end of the outbreak and is maintaining heightened surveillance.

On 17 November 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the BVD outbreak. The risk assessment categorizes States Parties into five groups based on population mobility from areas with community BVD transmission and response capacity.

The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the only State Party with currently documented community transmission, remains **very high**, reflecting the intensity and geographic expansion of the outbreak, ongoing undetected transmission, community deaths, health-care transmission, insecurity, laboratory constraints, gaps in community engagement and funding, and the continued potential for national spread.

The risk for States Parties with confirmed cases but without community transmission, including Kenya and Nigeria, is assessed as **high**, given the potential for onward and secondary transmission following importation, challenges in early detection, uncertainty around transmission chains, and the continued possibility of additional introductions.

The risk is also assessed as **high** for States Parties with substantial population connectivity to areas with community transmission, or with moderate connectivity but low response capacity. High population mobility, formal and informal cross-border movement, the possibility of undetected importation, variable surveillance and response capacities, and humanitarian and access constraints increase the likelihood of delayed detection and onward transmission.

The risk for States Parties with substantial connectivity but high response capacity is assessed as **low**. Although importation remains possible because of travel and other connections with affected areas, strong health systems and demonstrated outbreak-response capacities reduce the likelihood of sustained community transmission.

Finally, the risk for all other States Parties remains **low**. Transmission remains concentrated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with no evidence of sustained transmission beyond the country. However, further international exportation remains possible, requiring continued surveillance, preparedness, rapid detection and containment of any imported cases.

Based on the currently available information, WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, States Parties experiencing and/or responding to the public health event. The [Temporary Recommendations](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-08-2026-second-meeting-of-the-ihr-emergency-committee-on-the-epidemic-of-ebola-bundibugyo-virus-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-temporary-recommendations) issued to States Parties on 24 August 2026 underscore the importance of coordinated outbreak control, strengthened cross‑border collaboration, and sustained surveillance and preparedness to prevent further regional spread and ensure an effective public health response. Rapid recognition of cases, testing and optimized supportive care can reduce mortality, and improve community perceptions and acceptance of health care within the response.

Following the advice formulated by the IHR Emergency Committee regarding the epidemic of BVD in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Director-General of WHO determined that the event continues to constitute a PHEIC. An updated set of Temporary Recommendations will be issued to States Parties, and this will be reported in the next Disease Outbreak News publication.

fields.title: Multi-country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak Situation Report No. 27 (9 - 15 November 2026)
fields.body:
**IOM REGIONAL RESPONSE AT A GLANCE**

During the reporting period (9–15 November 2026), IOM supported 3,729,851 traveller screenings, bringing the cumulative total to 79,831,882 screenings since the start of the outbreak. Thirty-nine alerts were identified through IOM-supported surveillance – 28 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), 1 in Uganda and 10 in the Central African Republic (CAR) – bringing the cumulative total to 1,034 alerts.

At IOM-supported points of entry (PoEs) and points of control (PoCs) in DRC, five deceased persons were intercepted and referred for sample collection and safe and dignified burial, bringing the cumulative total to 271. One confirmed Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) case was reported in a displacement site, bringing the cumulative number of confirmed cases detected through IOM-supported surveillance to 73.

IOM reached 3,073,123 people through risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) during the reporting period, bringing the cumulative reach to 68,933,505 people since the start of the outbreak.

fields.title: Central African Republic: Situation Report No. 94, as of 17 November 2026
fields.body:
**HIGHLIGHTS**

- Despite a still volatile context, some humanitarian movements have resumed around Zémio.
- Infrastructure has been installed in Ouham-Pendé to help prevent agro-pastoral conflicts and reduce tensions between herders and farmers.
- 3,900 students received school kits in Kaga-Bandoro and M’brès.

**GENERAL CONTEXT**

Haut-Mbomou Prefecture – South-East

The security situation remains volatile in the Zémio area, despite a relative improvement recently observed along certain roads around the town. In this context, humanitarian actors have gradually resumed some movements and activities in areas affected by movement restrictions that have been in place since September. A limited resumption of civilian movement has also been observed on the main road corridors, while staff from peripheral health facilities have been able to travel to Zémio to replenish medical supplies. No incidents have recently been reported on these routes. A humanitarian organization also conducted movements along the Zémio-Dembia axis to carry out assessments. Given the continuing volatility of the security environment, humanitarian partners are closely monitoring developments and maintaining existing security and risk-management measures.

**HUMANITARIAN NEEDS AND RESPONSE**

**Health**

Haute-Kotto Prefecture – Central

On 11 November, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and its partner International Medical Corps (IMC) concluded their campaign providing comprehensive care for women living with obstetric fistula. A total of 33 patients received specialized treatment in Bria, with an 88 per cent success rate. 15 other patients faced transportation challenges in reaching Bria from Ndele in Bamingui-Bangoran Prefecture. To improve access to services in that area, a second two-week campaign is being conducted in Ndele from 12 to 26 November 2026.

**Multi-sector**

Vakaga Prefecture – North-East

On 11 November, the NGO COHEB, under a labour-intensive work project implemented through the Emergency Project to Support the Stabilization and Recovery of Refugees and Host Communities in the Lake Chad Basin (PASRRC), distributed cash assistance to 400 beneficiaries, including 150 Sudanese refugees and 250 members of host communities. Through the cash-for-work approach, each beneficiary received 30,000 CFA francs to support livelihoods and meet priority household needs.

fields.title: République centrafricaine : Rapport de situation N° 94 au 17 novembre 2026
fields.body:
**FAITS SAILLANTS**

- Malgré un contexte toujours volatil, certains mouvements humanitaires ont repris autour de Zémio.
- Des infrastructures pour prévenir les conflits agro-pastoraux et réduire les tensions entre éleveurs et agriculteurs dans l’Ouham-Pendé.
- 3 900 élèves reçoivent des kits scolaires à Kaga-Bandoro et M’brès.

**CONTEXTE GÉNÉRAL**

Préfecture du Haut-Mbomou – Sud-Est

La situation sécuritaire demeure volatile dans la région de Zémio, malgré une accalmie relative observée récemment sur certains axes routiers autour de la ville. Dans ce contexte, les acteurs humanitaires ont progressivement repris certains déplacements et activités dans les zones affectées par les restrictions de mouvement en vigueur depuis septembre dernier. Une reprise limitée de la circulation des populations civiles a également été observée sur les principaux axes concernés, tandis que le personnel des formations sanitaires périphériques a pu se rendre à Zémio pour s’approvisionner en médicaments. Aucun incident n’a été rapporté récemment sur ces itinéraires. Une organisation humanitaire a par ailleurs effectué des déplacements sur l’axe Zémio-Dembia afin de conduire des évaluations. Compte tenu de la volatilité persistante du contexte sécuritaire, les partenaires humanitaires continuent de suivre étroitement l’évolution de la situation et maintiennent les mesures de gestion des risques et de sécurité en vigueur.

**BESOINS ET RÉPONSE HUMANITAIRE**

**Santé**

Préfecture de la Haute-Kotto – Centre

Le 11 novembre 2026, le Fonds des Nations Unies pour la population (UNFPA) et son partenaire International Medical Corps (IMC) ont clôturé leur campagne de prise en charge holistique des femmes vivant avec une fistule obstétricale. Au total, 33 patientes ont bénéficié de soins spécialisés à Bria, avec un taux de réussite de 88 %. 15 autres patientes ont été confrontées à des difficultés de déplacement pour atteindre Bria depuis Ndele dans la préfecture du Bamingui-Bangoran. Afin d’améliorer l’accès à ces services dans cette préfecture, une seconde campagne de deux semaines a lieu à Ndele du 12 au 26 novembre 2026.

**Multisectoriel**

Préfecture de la Vakaga – Nord-Est

Le 11 novembre 2026, l’ONG COHEB, dans le cadre du projet de Travaux de haute intensité à main d’œuvre (THIMO) mis en œuvre à travers le Programme d’appui d’urgence à la stabilisation et au relèvement des réfugiés et des communautés hôtes dans le bassin du Lac Tchad (PASRRC), a procédé à une distribution monétaire au profit de 400 bénéficiaires, dont 150 réfugiés soudanais et 250 membres des communautés hôtes. A travers l’approche « travail contre rémunération », chaque bénéficiaire a reçu une assistance en espèces de 30 000 FCFA, visant à soutenir les moyens d’existence et à répondre aux besoins prioritaires des ménages vulnérables.

fields.title: The Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak in Africa: Six-Month Situation and Response Report
fields.body:
## **Executive summary**

This report examines the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak and the continental response from the declaration on 15 May 2026 to the evidence available for preparation of the six-month milestone on 15 November. It integrates pathogen and transmission knowledge, zoonotic origin and One Health, epidemiology, clinical care, operational performance, country experiences, research, financing, logistics, essential health services, social consequences and preparedness.

The principal finding is that substantial response capacity was mobilized, but persistent transmission and mortality indicate that this capacity did not consistently translate into sufficiently early detection, timely access to care, complete identification of transmission networks and reliable local service delivery in DRC. The introduction that began the outbreak also remains unexplained, so the risk of further spillover in the affected landscape persists independently of progress against human-to-human transmission.

### **Key findings that should guide the next phase**

**1. The burden remains overwhelmingly concentrated in the DRC.** Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria provide distinct experiences of managing cross-border or travel-associated infection. Their outcomes should be assessed against their own case histories and observation periods. France’s imported case and medical evacuations to other countries belong in a separate international account so that the same patient is not counted twice.

**2. Early growth was exceptional, but historical comparison requires matched definitions.** The early reported burden substantially exceeded burden observed during the comparable early periods of major 2014 and 2018 Ebola epidemics, although direct quantitative comparison is constrained by differences in case categories included, uncertainties in disease onset and official detection and declaration, ascertainment and observation intervals. Historical comparisons should therefore preserve the original case classifications and reporting periods.

**3. Contact tracing misses most new cases:** Only 11% of confirmed cases (1,146 of 10,659 with onset from week 19 to week 45) came from the contact lists, against a target of 95%. The response found the other 89% outside those lists, which means many transmission links were identified too late to list and monitor the contacts. The daily contact follow-up \[text continues beyond the visible page\].

### **Five headline numbers in the analytical snapshot**

By 8 November 2026, five countries had reported 11,021 confirmed cases and 5,358 deaths, a crude case-fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.6%.

The DRC carries almost all of this burden, with 10,990 cases and 5,354 deaths (CFR 48.7%). Uganda reported 20 cases and 2 deaths, Kenya 9 and 2, Nigeria 1 imported case and no deaths, and France 1 imported case and no deaths.

In the DRC, 67 health zones in eight provinces have reported at least one confirmed case, and 51 of 67 health zones reported a case in the last 21 days.

National notifications have held at about 460 to 480 confirmed cases a week since late September; the epidemic is a sustained plateau and not yet declining.

fields.title: Operational Update - Central African Republic - July - September 2026
fields.body: UNHCR's operations in the Central African Republic (CAR) are built on protection through presence, the cornerstone of the humanitarian response. Amid volatile security conditions and the spillover of the crisis in Sudan, UNHCR also remains ready to respond to emergencies. Durable solutions are another top priority supporting the voluntary, safe, and dignified return of Central African refugees, their sustainable reintegration, and their contribution to national development. Together with the Government of CAR and its partners, UNHCR provides protection and multisectoral assistance to internally displaced people (IDPs) and refugees, including Sudanese and Chadian refugees, while promoting durable solutions for Central Africans returning home. Its work is aligned with national priorities: the National Development Plan, the National Strategy for Durable Solutions and the Solutions Support Platform established under the 2022 Yaoundé Declaration.

fields.title: République Centrafricaine (RCA) Mise à jour opérationnelle Trimestrielle | Juillet - Septembre 2026
fields.body:
Les opérations du HCR en République centrafricaine (RCA) reposent sur la protection par la présence, pilier central de la réponse humanitaire. Dans un contexte marqué par la volatilité sécuritaire et les répercussions de la crise soudanaise, le HCR reste également mobilisé pour répondre aux urgences.

La recherche de solutions durables constitue une autre priorité majeure, notamment l’appui au retour volontaire, sûr et digne des réfugiés centrafricains, ainsi qu’à leur réintégration durable et à leur contribution au développement national.

Aux côtés du Gouvernement centrafricain et de ses partenaires, le HCR assure la protection et une assistance multisectorielle aux personnes déplacées internes (PDI) et aux réfugiés, notamment soudanais et tchadiens, tout en promouvant des solutions durables pour les Centrafricains de retour. Les interventions s’alignent sur les priorités nationales : le Plan national de développement, la Stratégie nationale pour les solutions durables et la Plateforme d’appui aux solutions issue de la Déclaration de Yaoundé de 2022.

fields.title: Chad : Humanitarian Situation in Lac Situation Report N° 02 (30 October 2026)
fields.body:
*This report was produced by OCHA in collaboration with the authorities and humanitarian partners. It primarily covers the period from 1 to 30 October 2026 and incorporates findings from the July 2026 mid-term evaluation of the response to internally displaced persons (IDPs). The next report will be published at the end of November 2026.*

**KEY POINTS**

- 307,206 displaced people in the province according to IOM Round 26, including 268,064 IDPs, 17,100 returnees, and 22,042 former IDPs who have returned.
- More than 75,000 IDPs have been hosted across 16 sites in the Fouli and Kaya departments since May 2026. New population movements continue to be reported and remain under verification.
- An encouraging improvement in the cholera situation was observed between 13 and 26 October, followed by a resurgence of 12 new cases in Kiskawa. However, the case fatality rate remains high (5.78%), well above the WHO emergency threshold, requiring the need to strengthen prevention, surveillance, and WASH interventions.
- The areas of Liwa, Kiskawa, Kadoulou, and Daboua are among those most exposed to security risks. This insecurity directly contributes to population displacement, loss of livelihoods, and reduced access to basic services.
- Four incidents were reported in the departments of Fouli and Kaya, affecting several civilians and resulting in dozens of deaths as well as abductions, a toll that would have been even higher without the intervention of the defense and security forces.
- Despite the scale of needs, the protection sector remains the least covered, with only 0.3% of targeted people assisted.
- A concerning deterioration in livelihoods has been observed linked to low rainfall.
- US$10.6 million has been mobilized through humanitarian emergency funding mechanisms, including CERF, the Regional Humanitarian Fund, and anticipatory action, to support the response.
- Significant humanitarian needs remain unmet due to insufficient funding, particularly in protection, shelter and site management, education, health and nutrition, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), and food security.
- The revitalization of the Grand Cadre Nexus and the review of convergence zones offer an opportunity to strengthen integrated investments by linking emergency response, access to essential services, social cohesion, and resilience.

fields.title: Cluster Protection RDC : Aperçu des violations et abus des droits humains dans la province du Nord-Kivu, octobre 2026
fields.body:
*En octobre 2026, la situation de protection au Nord-Kivu est restée critique, marquée par une intensification des affrontements dans les territoires de Masisi, Walikale et Rutshuru. Cette situation se serait traduite par l’usage d’armes lourdes et de frappes de drone, des représailles contre les civils ainsi que des déplacements forcés.*

**FAITS SAILLANTS DE LA PÉRIODE**

**Intensification des hostilités** : Des affrontements auraient opposé un groupe armé à une coalition de groupes armés dans les territoires de Masisi et de Walikale, et des frappes de drone auraient visé Binza (Rutshuru).

**Déplacements forcés** : Près de 2 580 ménages (environ 12 900 personnes) auraient été déplacés, dont 546 à Busanza (Rutshuru) et 450 à Kasake (Masisi).

**Engins explosifs** : Des projectiles tombés sur Kasake auraient fait 4 morts et 6 blessés, et des engins explosifs largués sur Kangati auraient tué 2 garçons.

**Représailles et riposte Ebola** : Des enlèvements contre rançon accompagnés de meurtres et des attaques de structures sanitaires à Butembo et Beni auraient été commis.
